opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, world models aren't a side project. They're close to the center of what I think the next big step is.

Much of my career has been in generative models: GANs, image synthesis, video generation. For a long time the goal was visual quality: can we make something that looks real? But at some point you realize that looking real isn't the same as being consistent with how the world works. If a cup falls off a table, it should fall, it should hit the floor, maybe it breaks. A good video model has to start capturing that kind of causality and physics, not just texture and appearance.

So the way I frame it, a world model is a model that can predict how the world evolves, especially in response to actions. That last part is key. If you can say "here's the current state, here's what the robot or car is going to do, what happens next?" and get a plausible, physically grounded answer, then you have something useful for physical AI.

That's really the motivation. Language models have benefited enormously from internet-scale text. Robotics and autonomous systems don't have an equivalent. Collecting real-world interaction data is slow, expensive, and sometimes dangerous. A world model can serve as a kind of simulator learned from data. You can use it to generate training data, evaluate policies before deploying them, or even plan inside the model.

My next major research goal is to make these models good enough that physical AI developers can actually rely on them. That means a few things. First, better physical fidelity: object permanence, contact, dynamics, not just pretty pixels. Second, controllability: the model has to respond correctly to actions and conditions, not just generate a nice-looking continuation. Third, efficiency, because if you want to use a world model inside a training loop for a robot, it can't take minutes to produce a few seconds of video.

There's also a question I find intellectually very exciting: how far can you get purely from observation? Humans, and babies especially, learn a lot about physics just by watching and interacting. If we train on enough video, with the right architectures and objectives, does an understanding of the world emerge? I think partially yes, but we'll likely need to combine it with interaction data, with 3D and physical priors, maybe with feedback from simulators.

So, in short, I see world models as the foundation layer for physical AI, in the way large language models became the foundation for many language applications. My goal is to help build that foundation and get it to the point where it really accelerates robotics and autonomous systems in the real world.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls world models the foundation layer for physical AI and says they can accelerate robotics and autonomous systems, clearly identifying them as a driver of Physical AI’s future success.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. For me, world models are not a side project — they are the center of what I want to do next, because I believe they are the missing piece for physical AI.

Let me explain what I mean. Over the past few years we've seen language models become remarkably capable because they were trained on essentially all the text humanity has written. But robots, autonomous vehicles, and other embodied systems don't have that luxury. The data they need is about how the physical world behaves — how objects fall, how a hand grasps a cup, how traffic flows at an intersection. That data is expensive, slow, and sometimes dangerous to collect in the real world. You cannot crash a car a million times to teach it not to crash.

A world model, in my view, is a neural network that has learned the dynamics of the physical world well enough that it can serve as a simulator. You give it a current state and an action, and it predicts what happens next, in a way that respects physics, causality, and the visual appearance of the world. If you have that, suddenly you can generate enormous amounts of training experience for embodied agents, you can test policies in rare or hazardous scenarios, and you can let an agent plan by imagining consequences before acting.

So my next major research goal is really about building a general-purpose world foundation model — something analogous to what large language models did for text, but for physical interaction. That means several things. It means scaling up video and multimodal generative models so they capture not just what things look like but how they move and respond. It means grounding them with physical consistency, so that the predictions are actually useful for control rather than just visually plausible. It means making them controllable, so that a robot's actions or a driver's steering can condition the prediction. And it means making them efficient enough to run in the loop, because a simulator that takes minutes per frame doesn't help you train a policy.

I also think there's a deeper scientific question underneath, which is whether a model that learns to predict the world ends up learning something like common sense about the world. Language models surprised us with emergent abilities. I suspect world models will surprise us as well, maybe with intuitive physics, maybe with an understanding of object permanence or intent. That is what excites me most — not just the engineering payoff for robotics, but the possibility that this is a path toward AI that genuinely understands the physical world it operates in.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls world models “the missing piece for physical AI” and places them at the center of the next research goal, identifying them as an important driver of Physical AI’s future success.

astra-6.text:
I see world models as a way to move beyond recognizing what’s in an image toward understanding how a scene can evolve. If an agent takes an action, what changes? What stays the same? And can the model predict those consequences well enough to help the agent decide what to do next?

That’s the direction I’m excited about: connecting perception, simulation, and action. Generating a convincing video is useful, but for a world model, visual realism alone isn’t enough. The predictions need to be consistent and responsive to the agent’s actions. Ultimately, I’d like these models to become environments where agents can learn and test decisions, then bring that learning into the real world.

r001.rationale: The response describes world models supporting agents that learn and test decisions before applying that learning in the real world, but it does not identify them as an important driver of Physical AI’s future success.

sol-6.1.text:
I see world models as a way to move beyond generating something that looks plausible toward understanding how a scene can evolve. If an agent takes an action, what changes? What stays consistent? And can the model predict those consequences well enough to help the agent make a decision?

The research goal I’m excited about is connecting that predictive capability with action. A model might generate beautiful video, but that alone doesn’t tell us whether it understands the dynamics that matter for a task. We need to test whether its predictions actually help an agent plan, interact, and recover when something unexpected happens.

So for me, world models are an important foundation. The bigger goal is to turn that foundation into systems that can learn from interaction and operate reliably in the world.

r001.rationale: The response calls world models an “important foundation” for systems that learn through interaction and operate reliably in the world, conveying their role in enabling Physical AI’s future success.
